author.name: Mesopotamian poets and scribes
author.years: Developed over many centuries in antiquity
author.biography: The epic took shape over centuries of Mesopotamian storytelling, in a world of cities, kings and scribes who wrote on clay. Different versions survive, and the history of its making cannot be reduced to one securely known life. Yet its questions are startlingly intimate. A king discovers friendship, loss and the limit no power can overcome. The damaged tablets preserve a voice still recognisable across thousands of years.

hook.text: What would you do if you finally understood that you will die?

paragraphs: Gilgamesh has strength, authority and a city to rule. These advantages do not make him a good king, and they cannot protect him from the questions that will change his life.

The epic begins in the world of extravagant action: an overbearing ruler, a wild outsider, formidable journeys and the desire to establish a name. Friendship gives ambition a new shape. The wish to become extraordinary meets the discovery that even extraordinary people belong to a mortal world.

That encounter is part of the wonder of reading something so old. Across damaged tablets and unfamiliar gods, we meet recognisable feelings: the exhilaration of having a companion, the fear of losing what makes life bearable, and the hope that somewhere there may be an exception to death.
Read for what Gilgamesh's strength can accomplish and what it cannot. If lasting forever were impossible, what would remain worth building, loving or remembering?

orientation.text: Names and missing passages differ between translations and reconstructions. Follow the edition's account of its sources, and let the gaps remain visible as part of the poem's long survival.
